component.name: Cycle
component.summary: Indoor cycling training with smart trainer control

description.p: Cycle is a GNOME application for indoor cycling training. It connects to BLE smart trainers via FTMS, lets you run structured ERG workouts, records sessions with power, heart rate, and cadence data, and provides AI coaching advice through the Claude API.
Features:

ul.li: BLE smart trainer control via FTMS (ERG mode)
Structured workout player with power zone visualisation
Session recording: power, heart rate, cadence
AI coaching suggestions powered by the Anthropic Claude API

screenshot.caption: Riding a structured workout in ERG mode
Fitness, fatigue and form over time
The training week at a glance
Coaching notes written for the ride ahead
What a planned session asks of you
Pairing a smart trainer and sensors

description.p: Cycle can now measure your FTP instead of asking you to guess it. The Ramp Test in your workout library is ridden as a test: ten minutes easy, then the target rises by 8% of your FTP every minute until you cannot hold it. There is no finish line to reach — you ride until your legs run out, press "I'm done", and Cycle reads your FTP off your best minute.

While you ride it, the cockpit counts steps rather than counting down to an end that is not how the test finishes. The ladder now climbs far higher than before, so that if the FTP you are set to is well below your real one, you do not simply run out of steps and get told a number that is still too low.

Afterwards the summary offers the result: the FTP the test supports, how it compares with the one you had, and the best minute it came from. Nothing changes until you press the button. If you take it, your FTP is updated everywhere and the change is recorded in your FTP history alongside any you have made by hand.

Test rides are now marked as tests and kept out of the evidence Cycle uses to judge whether your FTP looks wrong. A ramp test is designed to end with you unable to hold the target, which otherwise reads as a hard session falling apart — so passing a test would have argued for lowering the very number you rode it to establish.

Also fixed: the AI Coach could read advice to "increase" your volume as a verdict to ease off, and then ease the session on your calendar, because the word increase contains the word ease. The ride summary no longer lists intervals you never reached as "No data", and no longer calls a test "Workout complete".

Please note: the first time you open this version, your training history is upgraded to a new format automatically. A backup is saved beforehand, in the same folder as your database, named cycle.db.pre-v7 followed by the date. Once upgraded, your data can no longer be opened by Cycle 0.10.0 or earlier — so if you ever go back to an older version, restore that backup alongside it.

Cycle now checks that a ride actually recorded properly before it counts. If your trainer drops off the air part way through, the ride still looks complete — but the training stress worked out from it is the intensity of the part that recorded, stretched over the whole time you were out. That number then feeds your Fitness and Fatigue for weeks, and the coach eases sessions that did not need easing.

A ride that did not record properly is now held back from your fitness figures, from the training load written into exported FIT files, and from what the AI Coach is shown. It says what looked wrong — how much of the ride lost power, a trainer reporting one fixed number, a reading no rider could produce — and what to check. The ride's own numbers are still there to look at.

If you know better, "Count it anyway" puts it straight back. The notice appears both on the summary you see when you finish and on the ride later, so you can decide while you still remember whether the trainer dropped out.
Also fixed: importing a training history saves a copy of the history it replaces, and that copy could be deleted moments after it was made, while older backups were kept instead.

Please note: the first time you open this version, your training history is upgraded to a new format automatically. A backup is saved beforehand, in the same folder as your database, named cycle.db.pre-v6 followed by the date. Once upgraded, your data can no longer be opened by Cycle 0.9.0 or earlier — so if you ever go back to an older version, restore that backup alongside it.

A training plan that has run its course now says so. Until now the Coaching page went on reporting the final week for ever, and the only way forward was to pay the AI Coach to build something new. It now names the day the plan ended and sums up what the block delivered — how many of its sessions you rode, and what your fitness did over it.

Beside that is "Start the Next Block", which builds the next four weeks from your own workout library using the same rules that already adjust your sessions. It costs nothing and sends nothing anywhere. It asks which days you train rather than guessing, and it leaves the days you are away alone. "Rebuild with AI" is still there if you would rather have the coach reconsider the whole plan.
Every building week in the new block includes a session hard enough to tell whether your FTP has moved — something the old plans did not reliably do.
Also fixed: asking the coach to rebuild a finished program used to request a single week and hid part of your time off from it, and the rebuilt plan never updated the dates it claimed to cover.

Days you have marked as time off are now left alone. When the AI Coach built or rebuilt a program it could put sessions straight onto a holiday, because it was told the dates you were away but not which week of the plan they fell in — so it had no way to avoid them.

It is now told both, and whatever it sends back is checked against your calendar before anything is written, so a day off stays a day off even if you book it after building the plan, or start the program on a different week than it was built for. Sessions left out are counted in the message that follows, rather than quietly going missing.

You can now watch something else while you ride. A new compact window shows the target and the power you are actually pushing, the countdown to the next interval, your heart rate and cadence, and the shape of the workout with your place in it — small enough to sit in a corner of the screen and readable without looking straight at it. Open it from the button on the ride screen, or press F10.

To keep it above your film, right-click its header bar — or hold Super and right-click anywhere on it — and choose "Always on Top". The window explains this the first time you open it, because an app on GNOME is not allowed to do it for you. Play the film in a maximised window rather than fullscreen, or it will sit above everything, pinned windows included.

Its background can be made more or less see-through from its own menu, and it remembers the choice along with its size. If a sensor stops reporting, it says so rather than leaving a number frozen where you would go on believing it.

Your coach is now told what day it is. It had one mention of the date, tucked into a heading, and no idea what day of the week it was — so it read a poor night from three days ago as last night's and wrote your morning around it. Every reading and every ride now says how long ago it was, in plain words.

Your step count is no longer reported a day late. This morning's steps are a running total of a day that has barely started, and the brief was handing them over as though they were a finished day — a morning after 7,000 steps opened by telling you that you had barely moved.

The numbers on the ride screen stay where they are. Crossing 100 W used to shove the whole cockpit sideways as the power reading grew a digit, and a sprint into four digits pushed it wider still. Units have moved up into the labels, so the figures themselves are bigger and steady.

The interval bar now empties as the interval runs down, instead of filling up while the clock beside it counted the other way. The line telling you which effort you are on is much larger — it is read from the saddle, and it was sized for a desk.

A session you rode from your program appears once on the calendar, not twice. The plan and the ride are both kept, as they must be, but the day now shows one line: the session, ticked off, at the load you actually did rather than the one that was estimated.

The numbers on the ride screen are much bigger. Your live power, and the heart rate, cadence and time beneath it, now grow to fill the space instead of staying small — so they can be read from the bike, at arm's length, while you are working hard.

The workout profile below them is now a strip rather than half the page. It used to take every spare pixel, which meant the larger your window, the bigger the chart grew and the more cramped the numbers looked. That is the other way round now.

Your coach now reads your wellness numbers properly. Each morning's HRV, resting heart rate and sleep score are measured against your own recent normal before they are sent, so a reading well below where you usually sit is pointed out as exactly that, instead of being left in a table for the coach to notice on its own. On this rider's own data it changed the advice for the day.
A reading from an earlier day is no longer described as this morning's. If your watch has not synced yet, your coach is now told which day the numbers are from, and to weigh them accordingly.

Your program can now suggest a slightly harder session, not only an easier one. On a morning when every recovery signal agrees you are ready — two mornings running, and on fresh form — it will offer to step today's session up one level. It will not touch a rest day, will not make an already hard session harder, and any sign at all that you are tired takes priority over it.

Your outdoor rides now count towards your plan. A day you actually trained on is no longer read as a missed session, whatever your plan had asked for that day — Cycle already holds the ride and no longer needs to be told about it. Nothing to tap, and nothing claims a road ride was an interval workout: opening the day shows you what it found. On this rider's own history it turned twelve missed sessions into eight, and only the genuinely skipped days are still counted.

When your program eases a session more than once, Undo now steps back one change at a time instead of jumping straight to the original. Before, the workout in between was lost and could not be reached from either direction. The row tells you where a press will land, while still naming what your program first asked for.
Opening a planned workout on the calendar now shows its power profile, so you can see the shape of a session where you decide whether to ride it — including on days you have already finished.
The load shown for a day you marked done no longer counts the same training twice when a real ride is sitting on it.

Please note: the first time you open this version, your training history is upgraded to a new format automatically. A backup is saved beforehand, in the same folder as your database, named cycle.db.pre-v5 followed by the date. Once upgraded, your data can no longer be opened by Cycle 0.6.1 or earlier — so if you ever go back to an older version, restore that backup alongside it.

Your ANT+ trainer is found again when you switch it on after opening Cycle. The ANT stick was only ever given 25 seconds to look for it, and once that ran out it quietly stopped listening for the rest of the session. A trainer woken a minute later was never seen, and pressing Scan did not bring it back — the only cure was restarting the app with the trainer already awake.

Cycle now keeps looking for as long as it is open, and if a search does stop, it notices and starts it again. Your heart rate strap and cadence sensor were affected in the same way and are fixed with it, so switching any of them on late now works.

You can now mark a planned session done yourself. Most riding happens away from this app, and until now a session only closed if you rode that exact workout here, on the day it was planned. Open a day on the calendar, or use the week list or your program card, and say the session happened. Ticked the wrong day, or changed your mind? Mark it not done again.

Marking a session done settles your plan and nothing else. It banks no training load: your fitness is worked out from rides that were actually recorded, never from the calendar. The day's load bar will fill in, because that is your plan's own accounting — but your fitness and form do not move.

Missed sessions are now counted over the last fortnight rather than over the whole program. If you started a plan with a date already in the past, it was counting sessions you never had the chance to ride, and that number could never come down however well you trained. Your coach is told the same fortnight, so it plans around the rider you are now rather than one who appears to have stopped.
On the week view, Undo now has a row of its own instead of sitting beside Apply, where it was not clear which change it would undo.
Your calendar now shows which sessions belong to your training program. Look for the accent dot in the month view; the week view spells out which week of the plan each session falls in.

When your program wants to ease a session — because your form is dug in, your resting heart rate is up, or you have missed a run of sessions — the calendar says so on the day itself, explains why, and lets you apply the change without leaving the page. Changed your mind? Undo puts the session back to what the plan originally asked for.
As before, adjustments only ever make a session easier, and only ever the next one: your form is worked out afresh every day, so deciding Thursday's session today would be guessing.
You can now plan a GPX route on the calendar, not just a workout. A planned route counts towards your projected fitness, using an estimate of what riding it will cost.
Anything you have planned can be moved. Drag it to another day in the week or month view, or open it and choose Reschedule. Sessions you have already ridden stay where they are.

Choosing what to schedule now shows you what you are picking: a workout's shape, length and training load, a route's distance and climbing, and what your training plan expects that day. There is a search box for finding something in a large library.
Cycle also asks for less access to your computer than before. It no longer requests any filesystem access at all.

Please note: the first time you open this version, your training history is upgraded to a new format automatically. A backup is saved beforehand, in the same folder as your database, named cycle.db.pre-v4 followed by the date. Once upgraded, your data can no longer be opened by Cycle 0.3.0 or earlier — so if you ever go back to an older version, restore that backup alongside it.
Cycle now shows screenshots in GNOME Software.
Updated a networking library to pick up an upstream thread-safety fix.
Fixed the first-run setup wizard, which opened too small and did not apply what you entered.
Initial release.
